title: The Model Call Surface
question: Who decides what happens after a model response?
scope: The model proposes; the runtime owns execution, verification, and quarantine.

steps.title: Supply the next call
steps.description: Messages, tool definitions, and limits enter the frozen model. A tool result becomes visible only when the runtime includes it in a later request.

steps.title: Inspect the envelope
steps.description: The response is a proposal with usage counts and a stop reason. A plausible payload alone does not authorize any action.

steps.title: Admit a tool action
steps.description: The tool-call branch passes through validation and authorization before sandbox execution. Its empirical result returns as a tool message.

steps.title: Separate ending paths
steps.description: An end-of-turn answer goes to verification; output stopped at its limit goes to quarantine. Neither path is permission to execute a partial proposal.

title: One Keyword, Two Token Sequences
question: Why can four spaces change the token budget?
scope: The printed IDs are specific to cl100k_base; they are not a universal tokenizer rule.

steps.title: Start from the same source line
steps.description: The unindented lexer identifies def and get_user_id as language structure. The byte-pair row instead splits the line into five vocabulary items.

steps.title: Add an indentation boundary
steps.description: The compiler records an indent separately from def. Its structural boundary is the dashed vertical line.

steps.title: Find the space absorbed into def
steps.description: The indented byte-pair sequence starts with token 262 and token 711. Token 711 crosses the lexer boundary because the fourth space joins def.

steps.title: Count the actual serialized sequence
steps.description: Only the four trailing tokens remain shared. The total changes from five to six, so character counts and compiler tokens cannot replace model-specific token counting.

title: Reject, Then Cancel
question: What does rejecting a stream guarantee, and what still depends on the service?
scope: The allowance is 4,096 steps and the pictured rejection is at step 96; avoided service work is conditional.

steps.title: Hold prefixes while parsing
steps.description: The runtime advances its parser without dispatching incomplete output. At step 96 the force key violates the schema.

steps.title: Reject locally and request cancellation
steps.description: The runtime records rejection and discards the partial proposal, then asks the service to cancel. Local refusal does not require a successful remote cancellation.

steps.title: Read the conditional saving
steps.description: The long dashed allowance represents up to 4,000 steps not run, not guaranteed saved execution. It depends on the service receiving and honoring the request.

steps.title: Keep the two outcomes separate
steps.description: The payload remains undispatched even if remote decoding continues. Batch departure and KV-cache release belong to the honored-cancellation branch.

title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
question: How does a grammar mask restrict the next sampled token?
scope: This query-tool automaton enforces syntax; it does not establish data truth or authorization.

steps.title: Compile the tool language
steps.description: The schema is compiled once into parser states with associated vocabulary masks. The current state selects the mask used at this decode step.

steps.title: Remove illegal continuations
steps.description: The raw logits include fluent but invalid alternatives. Adding the state mask assigns invalid entries negative infinity before sampling.

steps.title: Advance after sampling
steps.description: The pictured opening brace is sampled from the legal support and advances the parser to q1. The next token uses that new state.

steps.title: Respect the guarantee boundary
steps.description: A grammatical query can still name a nonexistent table, use incorrect values, or be unauthorized. Those checks remain outside the token mask.

title: Selection Protects the State Budget
question: How can a long trajectory retain useful state without filling every prompt?
scope: The bars are a context-budget schematic, not measured byte occupancy or an exact additive tokenizer identity.

steps.title: Reserve room for an answer
steps.description: The hatched region remains reserved for output. Incoming context must fit below the Smax minus Kmax boundary.

steps.title: Watch observations crowd out state
steps.description: Appending every result grows the orange observation portion. By turn t+2 the green task state is squeezed.

steps.title: Select for the next decision
steps.description: The selected-working-set columns keep the state share while limiting observations staged into the next call. Selection changes the prompt, not what happened historically.

steps.title: Retain evidence outside the prompt
steps.description: Records can remain available behind handles and be retrieved when needed. Omitting them from the active prompt need not delete them.

title: Comprehension Falls with Context Length
question: Does a larger context allowance preserve comprehension?
scope: These are measured benchmark curves over the same rewritten stories, not a causal simulation of arbitrary prompts. Length categories are not equally spaced token increments.

steps.title: Compare like-for-like story questions
steps.description: At the shortest rewrite many curves begin near the top. Increasing the story length tests retention on the same question set rather than simply admitting a larger request.

steps.title: Read the cohort band
steps.description: The gray middle-half band widens downward through 60k. It summarizes the models scored at every length through that point, not all possible model behavior.

steps.title: Inspect the spread between models
steps.description: Some traces retain high accuracy while others decline substantially. Prompt capacity is therefore different from dependable comprehension of the material inside it.

steps.title: Keep endpoints and uncertainty intact
steps.description: Only the continuing colored traces provide the displayed evidence at 120k and 192k. Individual wiggles should not be treated as precise threshold locations or interpolated into a universal capacity rule.

title: Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token
question: Where does prefix reuse stop when the prompt changes?
scope: Exact token equality and compatible retained cache state are required; semantic similarity is insufficient.

steps.title: Organize by change rate
steps.description: Root instructions change rarely, trunk state changes less often than the latest leaf observation, and output has a separate reserve.

steps.title: Establish the cold prefix
steps.description: The cold-start call processes root, trunk r17, and leaf n. No previous compatible prefix is reused in this pictured call.

steps.title: Change the leaf
steps.description: Call n+1 keeps the root and trunk token prefix, so green reuse extends to the first changed leaf token. The later blue portion must be processed.

steps.title: Refresh the trunk
steps.description: Call n+2 changes trunk r17 to r18. Reuse now ends after the root even if later content resembles a previous request.

title: Invalidation Follows Recorded Dependencies
question: Which evidence becomes historical after editing pool.py?
scope: Propagation follows recorded dependencies; an old observation remains true of its recorded revision.

steps.title: Identify the changed source
steps.description: The write advances src/pool.py from r17 to r18. Its red outgoing dependencies identify which observations used that source.

steps.title: Keep old observations as history
steps.description: The source excerpt and controlled test run refer to r17. They remain historical evidence, but no longer establish the corresponding current-state claim.

steps.title: Reassess dependent conclusions
steps.description: Both affected observations supported the missed-notification hypothesis. The derived conclusion therefore needs reassessment rather than blind retention.

steps.title: Avoid unrelated invalidation
steps.description: The documentation excerpt and its API usage note are outside the changed dependency path. They keep their status in this recorded graph.

title: The Retrieval Contract
question: What must a retrieval result disclose before entering context?
scope: Access scope and revision are runtime bounds; a ranked hit is not automatically current or complete evidence.

steps.title: Declare the search boundary
steps.description: The runtime supplies scope, version, and limits; the model may propose terms. The search excludes r17 and material outside the allowed scope.

steps.title: Read status before reading hits
steps.description: The envelope reports the searched scope and revision together with complete, partial, or unavailable status. Limits and continuation information qualify what the search established.

steps.title: Stage only the needed payload
steps.description: The runtime stages returned items under the active payload budget. Returned evidence keeps path, range, revision, and provenance.

steps.title: Build a bounded next call
steps.description: The next model call receives selected evidence rather than an unqualified view of the entire repository. Search completeness and context selection remain separate properties.

title: Occurrences vs. Relationships
question: What can a structural edge tell us that a word match cannot?
scope: Static call edges indicate possible relationships, not observed execution; unresolved dynamic calls remain unknown.

steps.title: Find literal occurrences
steps.description: The notify postings include both src/pool.py and the failure log. A term occurrence does not establish a caller-callee relationship.

steps.title: Follow the resolved structure
steps.description: The test function calls the pool return method, which calls _available.notify(). Those directed edges answer a structural question beyond matching text.

steps.title: Preserve unresolved coverage
steps.description: The dashed CALLS ? branch ends at target unknown. Missing static resolution does not prove the runtime path cannot occur.

title: Searching an HNSW Graph
question: How does HNSW reach candidates without scanning every stored vector?
scope: The route is schematic; visited candidates and returned neighbors differ, and approximate search can miss true neighbors.

steps.title: Enter the sparse hierarchy
steps.description: The upper-layer entry point starts a greedy walk toward q. When no closer neighbor is available, the search drops to the matching node below.

steps.title: Refine the route
steps.description: The intermediate layer provides more vectors and another greedy hop. The dashed drop leads to the starting point for the base-layer beam.

steps.title: Explore a bounded candidate set
steps.description: Layer zero contains every vector, but the beam visits only part of the graph. efSearch controls exploration rather than making all nodes visible.

steps.title: Return from visited candidates
steps.description: Filled green nodes mark the returned best k; outlined green nodes were visited but not returned. Unvisited nodes cannot enter this result.

title: IVF-PQ Build and Query
question: How does IVF-PQ score compressed vectors?
scope: Printed dimensions and compression describe this illustrated configuration; code distances approximate full-vector distances.

steps.title: Encode a stored vector
steps.description: The FP16 vector is split into subvectors. Each subvector selects a codebook centroid, leaving one code index per subvector instead of the original values.

steps.title: Partition codes into coarse cells
steps.description: Each encoded vector is appended to an inverted list. At query time only the nprobe nearest coarse cells are chosen for scanning.

steps.title: Precompute query distances
steps.description: The query builds a lookup table of distances to subvector centroids. The table is shared across the candidate codes being scored.

steps.title: Sum code lookups
steps.description: Each candidate score sums the entries named by its stored indices. This cuts stored-vector traffic while introducing quantization and cell-selection approximation.

title: Filtering Inside a Graph Walk
question: Why can an access mask make an eligible neighbor unreachable?
scope: Authorization must hold during retrieval; these alternatives do not grant access to masked nodes.

steps.title: Observe the broken route
steps.description: The walk reaches the circled node and stalls when intermediate nodes are masked. Eligible green nodes near q may exist without an admissible route to them.

steps.title: Change the searchable topology
steps.description: Partitioning by scope builds traversal within the authorized subset. It changes the index organization rather than bypassing the scope mask.

steps.title: Provide an eligible entry
steps.description: An extra entry point can reach a surviving connected component. It addresses routing coverage without making excluded nodes retrievable.

steps.title: Scan when the subset is small
steps.description: For a selective eligible set, exact scoring can avoid graph reachability altogether. The cost depends on how many eligible vectors remain.

title: From Candidate Lists to Staged Evidence
question: How do lexical and dense retrieval combine without comparing incompatible scores?
scope: Fusion uses ranks over matched evidence identities; reranking remains bounded and does not establish truth.

steps.title: Generate complementary candidate lists
steps.description: Lexical ranking places B first while dense ranking places C first. Their raw scores need not share a numerical scale.

steps.title: Join the same evidence identity
steps.description: Scope, path, version, and span define a match. A span from r17 is not the same evidence item as an r18 span.

steps.title: Add rank contributions
steps.description: A appears in both lists and receives two reciprocal-rank contributions. Fusion rewards cross-list support without treating lexical and dense scores as interchangeable.

steps.title: Rerank a short pool
steps.description: The cross-encoder evaluates a bounded shortlist before staging evidence. Its work grows with pool size and pair length, so the shortlist is also a resource boundary.

title: Three Responses to a Source Edit
question: How can background indexing avoid serving stale content as current?
scope: The time labels are this figure’s reference estimates; freshness exclusion is a correctness rule, not a universal latency guarantee.

steps.title: Pay freshness on the write path
steps.description: Synchronous indexing blocks the write path while r18 is parsed and embedded. Queries then receive the refreshed entries.

steps.title: Find the unsafe window
steps.description: Without a generation check, background indexing leaves r17 admitted as current after r18 commits. Faster write completion does not make that claim correct.

steps.title: Exclude old entries immediately
steps.description: With exclusion, r17 is not admitted as current during the refresh window. The query uses a direct read or an explicitly partial result instead.

steps.title: Publish only if still current
steps.description: The rebuilt r18 entries become available only after a current-generation check. A later write would require another freshness decision.

title: The Prototype Loop vs. the Agent Harness
question: What does a harness add between a model proposal and a tool?
scope: The diagram compares control boundaries, not two measured implementations.

steps.title: Locate the direct dispatch
steps.description: In the prototype loop the model proposal reaches tools at once and the message list holds the state. Pause, spending, and approval have no enforcing boundary.

steps.title: Insert a guarded transition
steps.description: The same model now proposes to the harness. The harness owns trajectory records and admits calls through guarded transitions.

steps.title: Separate control from model inference
steps.description: Pause, cancellation, spending ceilings, and approval enter the harness independently. Budgets are reserved before work begins.

steps.title: Retain tool outcome ownership
steps.description: Only an admitted call reaches the tool, whose observation returns through the harness. Tool outcomes and model proposals remain distinct records.

title: Trajectory State Machine
question: Why does stopping admission differ from completing a trajectory?
scope: This is the chapter’s abstract trajectory state machine; FINALIZING settles or transfers remaining obligations.

steps.title: Admit from READY
steps.description: READY checks current guards before reserving a model call. A previous scheduling decision does not authorize later work automatically.

steps.title: Represent external waits
steps.description: WAITING_TOOL tracks an admitted tool operation; AWAITING_APPROVAL holds a proposal before dispatch. Approved work still requires guards to pass.

steps.title: Pause without finalizing
steps.description: PAUSED admits no new work but remains a live state with a resume path. It is distinct from a completed or canceled result.

steps.title: Stop admission and settle
steps.description: Completion, cancellation, deadlines, and budget limits route through FINALIZING. Only after checks and settlement does the trajectory enter an absorbing outcome.

review_notes: Visually inspected PNG rendered directly from the canonical source SVG; mapped original panels and labels without redrawing the figure. Region bounds inspected as overlays against the canonical artwork.

title: The Approval Gate
question: What exactly does human approval authorize?
scope: Approval binds a particular proposal and scope; it is not blanket permission or proof of task acceptance.

steps.title: Bind the actual action
steps.description: The reviewer sees the exact r18 proposal and named check records. Destination, evidence, preconditions, expiry, and requesting trajectory are part of what is approved.

steps.title: Keep approval immutable
steps.description: The approval digest binds every displayed field. Changing the artifact or arguments changes what must be approved.

steps.title: Wait without executing
steps.description: The proposal stays in AWAITING_APPROVAL while a reviewer decides. The model is not asked to approve its own action, and denied or expired requests are refused.

steps.title: Recheck at dispatch
steps.description: An approval is usable only while current and while capacity and guards allow admission. An approved request with no capacity stays held; a stale one is refused.

title: A Runaway Loop and the Budget That Ends It
question: Why are valid individual calls insufficient to bound a failing trajectory?
scope: The loop is an illustrative failure pattern; the harness budget is maintained outside model context.

budget.label: Actual reserved proposed and finalization budget

steps.title: Follow a locally valid failure loop
steps.description: The model proposes a variant, the test fails, and the error is appended before another retry. Each call may be well formed and within its individual limits.

steps.title: Observe history without progress
steps.description: Later contexts carry more error observations while the original task remains. A growing transcript alone supplies no termination guarantee.

steps.title: Account outside the prompt
steps.description: The harness sums actual, reserved, proposed, and finalization resources against the allowance. Model-visible history is not the authoritative budget ledger.

steps.title: Refuse new work at the boundary
steps.description: When the proposed admission exceeds the budget or deadline, the harness routes to FINALIZING to settle or transfer obligations. Refusal does not erase work already dispatched.

review_notes: Visually inspected PNG rendered directly from the canonical source SVG; mapped original panels and labels without redrawing the figure. Region bounds inspected as overlays against the canonical artwork.

title: Failed Runs Take More Calls
question: What can successful-run call counts tell us about a candidate ceiling?
scope: These are post-hoc distributions of unconstrained runs. Enforcing a visible ceiling can change agent behavior, so a candidate policy still needs a new evaluation.

steps.title: Read cumulative call distributions
steps.description: In the first panel the accepted solid curve rises before the failed dashed curve. At a given call count, more eventual successes have already finished.

steps.title: Inspect what the ceiling removes
steps.description: The first panel’s vertical ceiling would halt 31% of eventual failures and 9% of eventual accepted runs. This is a retrospective trade-off, not proof of those outcomes under a changed policy.

steps.title: Avoid transferring a threshold blindly
steps.description: SWE-agent 1.1 and OpenHands use the same named model but have different call distributions and ceiling locations. The harness configuration affects the candidate limit.

steps.title: Evaluate a policy-specific ceiling
steps.description: The remaining configurations show the same need to separate failed and accepted tails. Choose a candidate from the appropriate configuration, then measure with that ceiling actually enforced.

title: Raising the Ceiling Helps Some Models, Not Others
question: Which models benefit when the enforced action ceiling increases?
scope: The points are benchmark observations at three enforced ceilings. Connecting lines do not measure intermediate ceilings or establish a universal optimal budget.

steps.title: Identify the intervention
steps.description: The horizontal axis lists enforced limits of 15, 50, and 100 actions. Each curve holds the named model fixed while the allowed action budget changes.

steps.title: Find continuing benefit
steps.description: The Sonnet 4.5 curve continues upward from 50 to 100 actions. For this measured configuration, additional opportunity still leads to more completed tasks.

steps.title: Find diminishing or negative return
steps.description: Sonnet 4, Sonnet 3.7, and computer-use-preview flatten or dip over the same interval. Extra actions do not uniformly improve task success.

steps.title: Separate success rate from budget response
steps.description: o3 starts lower but continues gaining. A model’s absolute success rate and its marginal response to a larger ceiling are different properties to measure.

title: Verdict-Aware Trace Selection
question: Why must evaluation accounting survive discarded traces?
scope: Tail selection preserves diagnostic detail selectively; it cannot repair records lost before capture.

steps.title: Capture under explicit limits
steps.description: Admitted trials enter through a minimizing and redacting capture boundary. Trace detail waits in a bounded buffer for late task verdicts.

steps.title: Select with precedence
steps.description: Failure or violation evidence takes priority, followed by pending or unknown outcomes and selected accepted runs. The priorities govern retained detail, not which trials existed.

steps.title: Acknowledge diagnostic losses
steps.description: Selected traces reach the trace store; other detail is discarded, and buffer pressure can cause eviction. Tail selection does not eliminate staging memory or ingress.

steps.title: Keep the denominator separately
steps.description: Every trial and recorded drop, eviction, or truncation reaches the accounting record outside the buffer. Evaluation rates must not use only the retained traces as their cohort.

review_notes: Visually inspected PNG rendered directly from the canonical source SVG; mapped original panels and labels without redrawing the figure. Region bounds inspected as overlays against the canonical artwork.

title: Staged Release and Its Hold Path
question: What changes when a release stage fails?
scope: Each stage has its own evidence criterion; the diagram does not claim that a small canary makes exposed tasks safe.

steps.title: Start with offline evidence
steps.description: Offline trials assign no live task to the candidate. Their paired acceptance interval must meet the declared margin before advancing.

steps.title: Distinguish copies from live work
steps.description: Shadow execution uses authorized copies, not ownership of the live task. Tool-call drift is a different criterion from the offline acceptance interval.

steps.title: Monitor a bounded live share
steps.description: The canary receives the indicated live share rho, with a sequential monitor and hard tripwires. A wider release requires every declared gate criterion.

steps.title: Hold admission without undoing effects
steps.description: An unmet criterion, problematic drift, or alarm stops new candidate admission. Outstanding work keeps its operation identities and owners and is settled by recovery, not rollback.

title: Observation Loss Masking
question: Does a zero loss mask mean the model ignores that segment?
scope: This simplified serialization omits a selected schema request and its returned schema; only the seven printed segments are inspected.

steps.title: Keep authorship distinct
steps.description: The supplied, policy, and environment lanes identify where each serialized segment originated. A tool result is an observation, not a policy action to imitate.

steps.title: Select corrected policy responses
steps.description: The corrected tool call and final response carry mask one. The refused proposal and environment messages carry zero direct imitation loss.

steps.title: Retain conditioning context
steps.description: The green attention path reaches earlier segments, including those with zero direct loss. Later selected targets can still update the parameters that encode that context.

steps.title: Avoid training an environment impersonator
steps.description: Leaving observations out of direct policy loss preserves the conditional action objective. It does not remove observations from the model input.

title: Observations Dominate Recorded Trajectories
question: Why is transcript volume larger than eligible policy supervision?
scope: Bars measure pooled transcript characters with each message counted once, not tokenizer counts, repeated prompt ingestion, or compute spent.

steps.title: Partition one recorded transcript
steps.description: The first bar separates supplied prompt, environment observations, and generated model output. The three shares describe characters in the stored record.

steps.title: Find where most storage comes from
steps.description: The second configuration’s long green region shows observations dominating its transcript. Tool output can occupy most of the record without being a policy action to imitate.

steps.title: Distinguish eligibility from selection
steps.description: The fourth configuration has a larger dark model-output share, but not every generated token is a valid training target. Refused or incorrect proposals still require target selection.

steps.title: Keep the measurement denominator
steps.description: The legend and axis describe character shares, chosen because tokenizers differ across configurations. These bars cannot be read directly as token budgets or training compute fractions.

title: Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples
question: Why is a causal mask insufficient for independent packed examples?
scope: The grids teach attention isolation; skipping masked kernel work is a separate implementation property.

steps.title: Find the packed example boundary
steps.description: Both eight-position grids place example one before example two. The ordinary causal rule lets every second-example query score earlier first-example keys.

steps.title: Inspect the unintended context
steps.description: The red lower-left rectangle is the leak: example two can read context it will not have when served independently.

steps.title: Mask across example identity
steps.description: The block-diagonal version assigns that cross-example rectangle negative infinity before softmax. Boundary offsets define which keys belong to the query’s example.

steps.title: Preserve each example’s causal history
steps.description: The two blue causal triangles remain valid inside their own blocks. Correct masking establishes isolation, not a guaranteed throughput improvement.

title: Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling
question: How does on-policy labeling address states missing from reference demonstrations?
scope: The displayed bounds retain their distinct error distributions and bounded-disadvantage assumption; aggregation alone does not equalize distributions.

steps.title: Locate the coverage gap
steps.description: The learner leaves the recorded reference path at s2. Subsequent dashed red states have no recorded correction even if imitation error on reference states is small.

steps.title: Collect states the current policy visits
steps.description: A labeling round runs the current policy with the stated reference mixture, records visited states, and obtains proposed corrective labels.

steps.title: Verify before retaining a label
steps.description: A sandbox continuation must pass the verifier before aggregation. Rejected proposals follow the discard path rather than entering training merely because a labeler produced them.

steps.title: Select recovery rather than injected error
steps.description: In the fault-injected record, the error has mask zero; diagnosis and corrective call have mask one. Retraining broadens coverage, while the learner-state bound still requires its printed assumptions.

scope: Keep the complete whole-system synthesis as the static reference; earlier figures teach individual mechanisms.
